articles.title: Your LED Light Takes a Few Seconds to Turn On? It's the Driver Capacitor, Not the LEDs
articles.excerpt: Last week a customer called about the light on his parents' balcony. "It's broken," he said — flip the switch at night and you wait two or three seconds before anything happens. He wanted a quote for…
articles.body: Last week a customer called about the light on his parents' balcony. "It's broken," he said — flip the switch at night and you wait two or three seconds before anything happens. He wanted a quote for a replacement LED panel. I asked him to do one thing: switch it off, then on again immediately. It came on instantly. So the light wasn't broken. That sequence — slow after sitting off, instant right after being on — has already completed most of the diagnosis: the problem is in the driver's startup stage, nothing to do with the LED chips, and swapping the panel is money down the drain . Once winter arrives, calls like this come in waves. Three Kinds of "Slow" — Only One Is a Fault Soft-start: normal.

articles.title: Crypto Trading Bots That Work: How to Tell Honestly
articles.excerpt: People searching for "crypto trading bots that work" usually want a name, but no bot "works" in general. A bot only works if it shows a measurable edge after fees and slippage, over enough trades, in…
articles.body: People searching for "crypto trading bots that work" usually want a name, but no bot "works" in general. A bot only works if it shows a measurable edge after fees and slippage, over enough trades, in conditions it did not see during design, and most bots fail that test. This guide shows you how to run that test yourself, so you can judge any bot, including one you built, bought or found online. What "a crypto trading bot that works" actually means A bot that works is not one with a nice screenshot or a high win rate. It is a bot whose results survive four questions: Is there enough data? A few dozen trades can look brilliant by pure luck. Does it survive real costs? Fees, slippage and funding payments eat small edges first. Is it more than market beta?

articles.title: WAF is useful, but it does not provide complete protection: What Is a WAF ? Lessons from Incidents
articles.excerpt: Introduction: What Is a WAF ? A Checkpoint for Incoming Web Traffic A WAF (Web Application Firewall) is a security function that inspects HTTP/HTTPS traffic reaching websites and Web APIs. It applies…
articles.body: Introduction: What Is a WAF ? A Checkpoint for Incoming Web Traffic A WAF (Web Application Firewall) is a security function that inspects HTTP/HTTPS traffic reaching websites and Web APIs. It applies predefined rules to decide whether to allow, log, or block that traffic. A useful way to understand it is as a checkpoint placed in front of a website. Websites exposed to the internet receive requests that may contain well-known attack patterns, such as SQL injection and cross-site scripting (XSS). A WAF examines characteristics of these requests and can detect or block those that match known attack patterns, reducing the likelihood that some attacks reach the web application.

articles.title: How I Use Reusable Claude Skill Files to Run My Daily Work
articles.excerpt: Most people who use Claude every day have a messy folder or spreadsheet full of saved prompts somewhere on their laptop. I had one too. It had over a hundred prompts I copied from articles and threads…
articles.body: Most people who use Claude every day have a messy folder or spreadsheet full of saved prompts somewhere on their laptop. I had one too. It had over a hundred prompts I copied from articles and threads, and I almost never opened it. Every morning I still opened a blank chat, typed a rough paragraph explaining what I needed, and spent the next twenty minutes arguing with the output. One draft came back sounding like a stiff corporate press release. Another forgot my pricing model. By the twelfth message in the same thread, two annoying things always happened at once: Claude started losing track of instructions from the top of the chat, and I burned straight through a huge chunk of my 5-hour session limit. Most people don't realize how token math works inside a long AI chat.

articles.excerpt: Last week an AI agent fixed a bug for me in about five seconds. Clean fix, nice explanation, even a little summary at the end. And my first thought wasn't "wow." It was: "Huh. That one would've taken…
articles.body: Last week an AI agent fixed a bug for me in about five seconds. Clean fix, nice explanation, even a little summary at the end. And my first thought wasn't "wow." It was: "Huh. That one would've taken me three hours." Three hours of reading logs, adding console.log everywhere, questioning my career choices, and finally finding that one missing line. Those three hours were painful. They were also where I learned almost everything I know. So this isn't an "AI is bad" article. I use AI every day, and I like it. This is about what we gain, what we quietly lose, and why I sometimes catch myself missing the three-hour bug. 1. I'm glad I started coding before AI showed up I started coding back when there was no AI to ask.

articles.body: "We're building our own online store. Should we use Shopify or build it ourselves?" This is the question we get asked most. The usual answers are "Shopify is easier" or "open source gives you freedom". Both are true, and neither is enough to make the decision. This article gives you a framework you can apply directly. We build both Shopify stores and headless storefronts on MedusaJS, and we've hit the pitfalls on both sides, so we try not to favor either. What the two routes actually are Shopify / Shopify Plus : a SaaS e-commerce platform. The storefront, checkout, payments, inventory and orders are all hosted by the platform. You customize the storefront with themes (Liquid) and extend functionality with apps and APIs.

Reddit’s about to look and feel a lot different, and no, I’m not just talking about the new For You and Following feeds the platform announced yesterday. articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 29, 1991: NASA's Galileo spacecraft flies by asteroid Gaspra and snaps amazing photos while flying at 18,000 mph
articles.excerpt: On Oct. 29, 1991, the Galileo spacecraft flew by the asteroid Gaspra on its way to Jupiter. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Oct. 29, 1991, the Galileo spacecraft flew by the asteroid Gaspra on its way to Jupiter. Gaspra was the first asteroid to ever be visited by a spacecraft. Gaspra orbits near the inner edge of the asteroid belt . The Galileo spacecraft had been travelling through the asteroid belt for about two months before it reached Gaspra. Galileo was 990 miles (1,593 kilometers) away from Gaspra when it whizzed by, and it was travelling at a relative speed of about 5 miles (8 km) per second. The spacecraft took several photos of the asteroid and used an instrument called the Near-Infrared Mapping Spectrometer to study its chemical composition and other physical properties. Galileo determined that Gaspra has an irregular and elongated shape measuring about 12 miles long and 7 miles wide.

articles.title: Artemis II commander Reid Wiseman named deputy director for NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory
articles.excerpt: The leader of NASA's first mission around the moon in half a century is the last to announce what's next for him after retiring from active astronaut duty.
articles.body: The leader of NASA's first mission around the moon in half a century is the last to announce what's next for him after retiring from active astronaut duty. All four astronauts of the Artemis II mission, which flew around the moon in April, have hung up their spacesuits and moved on to greener pastures. NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL), managed by Caltech, announced yesterday that former NASA astronaut Reid Wiseman will step into the role of Caltech associate vice president and deputy director of JPL, beginning Nov. 30. "Reid has spent his career at the edge of what is possible, and he has the technical judgment, operational experience, and leadership to help push that edge farther," NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said in a JPL press release .
